# Day 23: the folder has 9 files, 6 are good
uv run python run_load.py
q: How does the loader treat the broken, empty, duplicate and unsupported files?
o: Skips each with a warning and loads the other 6
Stops at the first bad file
Loads all 9
why: Expected bad input is skipped loudly, so one bad file never stops the whole load.

q: 100 rows, split 60, 20, 20. What does each pile do?
o: Train learns, validation chooses, test measures once
All three train the model
Validation and test are the same

c:
baseline accuracy on validation: 0.55
rule accuracy on validation: 0.85
q: Why print the baseline at all?
o: To see if a model or rule really learned something
To make the output longer
Because scikit-learn requires it
why: A score only means something next to the dumbest sensible answer.

q: A train accuracy far above the validation accuracy. What is it called?
o: Overfitting
Underfitting
A baseline
why: The model memorises the practice rows and does worse on new ones.

c:
tried 200 models and kept the best on the test set: 0.66
the same model on fresh data it never saw: 0.54
q: Why is the first number too high?
o: The test set was used to pick the winner, so luck looks like skill
The fresh data is harder
The model was trained twice
why: Choose with validation, and look at the test set once.

o: 0, with no error: a silent bug
An error
why: Make failure loud: raise FileNotFoundError for a missing folder and keep a test on the count.

q: Scored on the rows it learned from. Is 1.0 good news?
o: No: it only says the model memorised the rows
Yes: a perfect model
Yes, if the data is clean
why: A fair score needs rows the model never saw.

q: Why do the scores differ for the same rule?
o: A pile of 20 rows is small, so a shuffle changes the score a lot
The rule changes with the seed
The data changes with the seed
why: A small pile gives a wobbly score. Do not read much into small differences.
